## Which ratios give a limiting sum? {#ss7-ratios .lim-lesson .lim-ratios}

Fix $a=1$. Compare the terms $a_n=r^{n-1}$ and the partial sums $S_n$.

<div data-module="limiting-ratios" class="lim-ratio-explorer"></div>

::: {.takeaway .fragment data-fragment-index="0"}

$$-1<r<1\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad |r|<1$$

:::

::: notes

Explore r=1/2, −1/2, 1, −1, 3/2 and −3/2. Each graph contains the first twelve discrete values with a common vertical scale within that selected case. Prediction first, then Reveal behaviour. Changing the ratio hides the explanation again. Reset returns to r=1/2 with hidden behaviour. Fractional negative ratios produce alternating terms and oscillating partial sums that still converge. At r=−1 the partial sums alternate 1,0 and have no single limit. At r=1 the terms stay at 1 and the sums increase without bound. For |r|>1, terms fail to approach zero. Finite plots suggest a pattern; the following algebra explains it. If asked about r=0, the recurrence gives 1,0,0,... and sum 1, within |r|<1. Use the final slide click to reveal the interval after exploring.

:::
